questions.hint: Factor both numerator and denominator to spot and cancel the common factor before substituting.

questions.explanation: Factor: \( \dfrac{x^{2}+(-9)x}{\sin 3x} = \dfrac{x(x+(-9))}{\sin 3x} \). Divide numerator and denominator by \( x \): \( = \dfrac{x+(-9)}{\left(\sin 3x\right)/x} \). As \( x\to 0 \), numerator \( \to (-9) \) and denominator \( \to 3 \) (by \( \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin kx}{x}=k \)), giving \( \dfrac{(-9)}{3} = -3 \).
questions.hint: Factor \( x \) out of the numerator, then divide numerator and denominator by \( x \) and use \( \lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin kx}{x}=k \).

questions.question: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{2\cos(a+h) - 2\cos a}{h} \), where \( a \) is a fixed real number.
questions.explanation: Factor out \( 2 \), then expand \( \cos(a+h) = \cos a\cos h - \sin a\sin h \). The expression becomes \( 2\left[\cos a\cdot\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} - \sin a\cdot\dfrac{\sin h}{h}\right] \). As \( h\to 0 \), this \( \to 2\left[\cos a\cdot 0 - \sin a\cdot 1\right] = -2\sin a \), matching \( 2\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x \) scaled by \( 2 \).

questions.question: If \( f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x+ 3} \), find \( f'(x) \) using first principles, for \( x \neq (-3) \).

topics.name: Intuitive Idea of a Limit — Left-Hand and Right-Hand Limits
topics.summary: A limit describes the value \( f(x) \) approaches as \( x \) nears a point \( a \), without necessarily reaching it. Because \( x \) can approach \( a \) from below or above, we split this into the left-hand limit \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) \) and the right-hand limit \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) \). The two-sided limit \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \) exists if and only if the LHL and RHL both exist and are equal; if they disagree, the limit does not exist at that point, even if \( f(a) \) itself is defined. This matters most for piecewise functions, where each branch must be evaluated separately near the junction, and for functions like the modulus function \( |x| \) or the greatest integer function \( [x] \), whose behaviour changes abruptly at certain points. For \( [x] \), at any integer \( n \), the LHL equals \( n-1 \) and the RHL equals \( n \), so the limit never exists at integers, even though \( [x] \) is defined there.
key_formulas: \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \) exists \( \iff \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) \)
For the greatest integer function \( [x] \) at integer \( n \): LHL \( = n-1 \), RHL \( = n \)
Piecewise \( f \): the LHL uses the branch valid for \( x < a \); the RHL uses the branch valid for \( x \geq a \)
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x) = \begin{cases} x+1, & x < 2 \\ 3x-1, & x \geq 2 \end{cases} \). As \( x \to 2^{-} \), \( f(x) \to 2+1 = 3 \). As \( x \to 2^{+} \), \( f(x) \to 3(2)-1 = 5 \). Since \( 3 \neq 5 \), \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) \) does not exist, even though both branches are individually well-defined at \( x=2 \).
common_mistakes: Assuming the two-sided limit exists without actually checking that the LHL and RHL agree
Evaluating only one side (often the branch that happens to contain \( x=a \)) and treating that as the full answer
Treating the greatest integer function \( [x] \) as if it were continuous, using \( [a] \) for both one-sided limits at an integer \( a \)

topics.name: Algebra of Limits — Polynomial and Rational Functions
topics.summary: The algebra of limits lets us evaluate a limit built from simpler pieces: the limit of a sum, difference, product, or quotient equals the corresponding combination of the individual limits, provided each individual limit exists (and, for a quotient, the denominator's limit is nonzero). For polynomials, this reduces to direct substitution, since polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions often produce a \( \frac{0}{0} \) indeterminate form at the point of interest; the fix is to factor numerator and denominator and cancel the common factor before substituting, never to substitute directly into the unsimplified expression. A closely related shortcut is \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a}\dfrac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a}=na^{n-1} \), which avoids factoring higher-degree polynomials by hand. When a limit involves a square root and produces a \( \frac{0}{0} \) form, multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate surd removes the indeterminacy in the same spirit. These techniques — factoring and rationalising — are the two main tools for taming \( \frac{0}{0} \) forms algebraically.
key_formulas: For \( \frac{0}{0} \) rational forms: factor and cancel the common factor before substituting
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3} \). Direct substitution gives \( \frac{0}{0} \), so factor: \( \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3} = \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3} = x+3 \) for \( x \neq 3 \). Taking the limit now gives \( 3+3 = 6 \).
common_mistakes: Substituting directly into a \( \frac{0}{0} \) form without factoring or rationalising first, and wrongly reporting the result as undefined or \( 0 \)
Cancelling the wrong factor, or cancelling only part of a factored expression
Forgetting to multiply the denominator by the conjugate too when rationalising a surd expression

topics.name: Limits of Trigonometric Functions
topics.summary: Two standard trigonometric limits underpin this topic: \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x}=1 \) and \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x}=0 \). Most trigonometric limit questions are variations built on top of these two results. When the argument of sine is scaled, as in \( \sin kx \), the trick is to multiply and divide by \( k \) so that the expression matches the standard form \( \dfrac{\sin kx}{kx} \), which tends to \( 1 \); the surviving factor of \( k \) is what remains. The same idea extends to \( \tan kx \) (via \( \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \)), to ratios like \( \frac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} \to \frac{a}{b} \), and to the squared cosine form \( \frac{1-\cos kx}{x^{2}} \to \frac{k^{2}}{2} \). Shifted versions, such as \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a}\dfrac{\sin(x-a)}{x-a}=1 \), follow from substituting \( u=x-a \). These results also connect directly to the derivatives of \( \sin x \) and \( \cos x \), which are proved using exactly these two standard limits together with the compound-angle formulas.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin 5x}{x} \). Write \( \dfrac{\sin 5x}{x} = 5\cdot\dfrac{\sin 5x}{5x} \). As \( x \to 0 \), \( 5x \to 0 \) too, so \( \dfrac{\sin 5x}{5x} \to 1 \), giving a limit of \( 5\cdot 1 = 5 \).
common_mistakes: Confusing \( \displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 \) with \( \displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\tan x}{x}=1 \) and misapplying one where the other is needed
Forgetting to multiply and divide by the coefficient inside the argument before applying the standard limit
Treating a trigonometric \( \frac{0}{0} \) form as automatically equal to \( 0 \) instead of applying the correct standard limit

topics.name: Derivative at a Point — First Principles and Algebra of Derivatives
topics.summary: The derivative of \( f \) at a point \( x \) is defined from first principles as \( f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \): the limit of the average rate of change over a shrinking interval as that interval's width \( h \) tends to zero. Applying this definition directly to polynomials, reciprocals, and square roots requires the same algebraic skills as rational and surd limits — expanding, combining fractions, and rationalising — to clear the \( \frac{0}{0} \) form before letting \( h \to 0 \). Once individual derivatives are established this way, the algebra of derivatives lets them be combined without repeating the whole process: the sum and difference rules simply add or subtract the pieces' derivatives, the product rule states \( \frac{d}{dx}[uv]=u'v+uv' \), and the quotient rule states \( \frac{d}{dx}\!\left[\frac{u}{v}\right]=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}} \). These rules mean that once the derivatives of a handful of building-block functions are known, complicated combinations can be differentiated directly, without returning to first principles each time.
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x)=x^{2} \). Then \( f(x+h)-f(x) = (x+h)^{2}-x^{2} = 2xh+h^{2} \). Dividing by \( h \) gives \( 2x+h \). Letting \( h \to 0 \) gives \( f'(x) = 2x \).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide by \( h \) (or by the denominator) before finally taking the limit
Sign slips while expanding \( (x+h)^{n} \) or combining fractions in the difference quotient
Applying the product or quotient rule with a sign or ordering error, such as using \( f'g-fg' \) instead of \( f'g+fg' \), or swapping the numerator terms in the quotient rule

topics.name: Standard Derivatives and Combined Limit–Derivative Applications
topics.summary: Rather than returning to first principles every time, a short table of standard derivatives covers the building-block functions used throughout this chapter and beyond: \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{n})=nx^{n-1} \), together with \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)=\cos x \), \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x \), \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\sec^{2}x \), \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x)=-\csc^{2}x \), \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)=\sec x\tan x \), and \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\csc x)=-\csc x\cot x \). Combined with the sum, product, and quotient rules from the algebra of derivatives, these let a wide range of expressions be differentiated directly, then evaluated at a specific point, without expanding a difference quotient by hand. A useful companion skill is recognising when a given limit of the form \( \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \) is simply \( f'(a) \) in disguise — such limits can be evaluated either by direct algebraic or trigonometric manipulation, or by identifying the underlying function and quoting its known derivative from the table, which is often the faster route and a useful check on the algebraic method.
key_formulas: \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)=\sec x\tan x \), \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\csc x)=-\csc x\cot x \)
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x) = x^{3}+\sin x \). By the power rule and the standard sine derivative, \( f'(x) = 3x^{2}+\cos x \). At \( x=0 \): \( f'(0) = 3(0)^{2}+\cos 0 = 0+1 = 1 \).
common_mistakes: Sign errors on the derivatives of \( \cos x \), \( \cot x \), and \( \csc x \), which each carry a minus sign
Forgetting to apply the product or quotient rule when a power term and a trigonometric term are multiplied or divided together, rather than just added
Misreading a first-principles limit as the function's value \( f(a) \) rather than recognising it as the derivative \( f'(a) \)
